sections.heading: 1 · Power Conversion & Power Quality in Sixty Seconds
bullets: Power = Voltage × Current (P = V·I), and wires waste power as heat proportional to current squared (I²R). Moving the same megawatt at higher voltage means less current, less loss, and thinner copper — this explains why storage systems run 1,000–1,500 V DC batteries and why fast-charger cables are liquid-cooled.

The grid is AC (alternating current — voltage easy to change with transformers); batteries, chips, and EVs are DC (direct current). Four machines bridge the two worlds: RECTIFIER (AC→DC), INVERTER (DC→AC), DC-DC CONVERTER (DC→different DC), TRANSFORMER (AC→different AC). Everything Sinexcel sells is a stack of these.

A PCS (power conversion system) is a rectifier and inverter in one bidirectional box: it inverts battery DC to grid AC when discharging and rectifies grid AC to battery DC when charging. It is THE interface between any battery and the grid — no PCS, no storage plant.

Modern converters chop current with semiconductor switches at tens of kilohertz; silicon-carbide (SiC) devices switch faster with less loss, shrinking hardware and pushing efficiency toward 99%. At utility scale, each 0.1% of efficiency is real money — lost twice (once charging, once discharging) and paid a third time in cooling.

Power QUALITY is about the shape of the wave, not just the amount of power: the grid wants a clean 50/60 Hz sine wave, and three things ruin it — harmonics (distorted current), reactive power (current doing no useful work), and voltage sags (brief dips). A whole product family exists to fix each one.

sections.heading: 2 · How Storage Plants and Factories Use Power Conversion Today
bullets: A battery storage plant (BESS) is a chain: cells → racks → a DC bus (1,000–1,500 V) → PCS → transformer → grid. The batteries are dumb energy tanks; the PCS is the gatekeeper that decides how hard to charge or discharge, follows grid-operator commands in milliseconds, and rides through grid faults without tripping.

Why grids pay for storage: grid frequency (50/60 Hz) is a live balance meter between supply and demand — too much demand and it droops, too much generation and it rises. Batteries earn by FREQUENCY REGULATION (injecting/absorbing power in under a second), peak shaving, shifting solar/wind to evening, and black start (re-energizing a dead grid). All of it flows through the PCS.

Factories poison their own power: rectifiers, variable-speed drives, LED drivers, and server power supplies draw current in sharp gulps instead of smooth sine waves. The distortion — HARMONICS, at multiples of the grid frequency — overheats transformers and neutral wires, trips breakers, and disturbs neighboring equipment. THD (total harmonic distortion) is the score; under 5% is the usual target.

Motors and transformers also draw REACTIVE power — magnetizing current that sloshes back and forth doing no net work but still occupying wires and transformers. POWER FACTOR (PF) = useful power ÷ total apparent power; utilities bill penalties below ~0.9 because low PF wastes their infrastructure.

VOLTAGE SAGS — dips lasting a few cycles when lightning hits a line or a big motor starts — are invisible to humans but fatal to precision industry: a 100-millisecond sag can scrap an entire semiconductor batch or crash a data hall. Riding through sags needs stored energy that reacts in milliseconds.

sections.heading: 3 · Sinexcel's Products Mapped Into the Chain
bullets: Storage PCS family — one architecture, many sizes: 30 kW modules for small systems; 135 kW Sirius for businesses and microgrids; cabinets that stack up to eight 215 kVA modules (215–1,725 kVA); the utility flagship StellaON at 1,250/1,575 kVA per unit; and a 40-ft container that packages PCS + medium-voltage transformer into a 10 MW plug-in station. Modularity means capacity is added like LEGO and a failed module is swapped, not the whole machine.

GRID-FOLLOWING vs GRID-FORMING is the key concept split: a grid-following inverter is a surfer — it locks onto the grid's existing wave and injects current into it (it cannot work without a live grid). A grid-forming inverter is a metronome — it creates the voltage wave itself, sets the beat, and other sources sync to IT. As coal/gas plants (whose spinning mass stabilized the grid for free) retire, grids increasingly require storage that can form, not just follow.

VSG (virtual synchronous generator) mode makes a grid-forming PCS impersonate a traditional spinning generator — synthetic inertia that resists frequency change — and enables black start (energizing a dead grid) and off-grid operation with 100+ PCS sharing the load in parallel. This is why 'grid-forming' shows up in every utility tender.

Numbers that matter in a PCS datasheet, and why: efficiency ~98.5–99% (paid on every kWh, twice); overload headroom like 1.5× (a PCS must briefly push extra current so breakers can trip properly during faults and big loads can start off-grid); DC window 1,040–1,500 V (matches high-voltage battery racks — I²R again); grid-code certifications per country (the real ticket to sell anywhere).

Power-quality trio: the ACTIVE HARMONIC FILTER (APF/AHF) works like noise-cancelling headphones for electricity — it measures the distorted current and injects the exact mirror-image in real time, cancelling harmonics to THD <5%. The SVG (static var generator) is the same inverter hardware aimed at reactive power — stepless power-factor correction to 0.99 in ~15 ms, where old capacitor banks switch in crude, slow steps. The AVC (active voltage conditioner) guards against sags: supercapacitors + a standby inverter inject the missing voltage within ~2 ms, holding equipment at 100% voltage even through a dip to zero.

Same trick, different targets: an AHF and an SVG are both fast inverters watching a current waveform — one cancels distortion, the other supplies magnetizing current locally. Recognizing that they, the PCS, and the EV charging module are all the same building block is the whole point of this company's catalog.

sections.heading: 4 · EV Charging and Microgrids Through the Same Lens
bullets: AC vs DC charging: an AC charger hands grid power to the car's small ONBOARD charger (hours to fill). A DC fast charger puts a big rectifier OUTSIDE the car and feeds the battery directly — the charger is essentially a one-way PCS. Charging speed then depends on how much rectifier you stack up.

The CHARGING MODULE is the atom of fast charging: a 20–40 kW AC→DC brick (SiC-based, ~97% efficient, wide 50–1,000 V output to cover both 400 V and 800 V vehicle packs). Chargers are built by paralleling modules — 24 modules ≈ 480 kW — so the same merchant module sells inside the company's own chargers and to rival charger makers.

DISTRIBUTED architecture separates the power bank (one cabinet full of modules) from the dispensers (the posts with cables). Software allocates modules to whichever car can absorb power — batteries charge fast when empty and taper when full, so fixed per-post power sits idle. Dynamic allocation claims ~97% utilization of installed power.

Why megawatt charging needs liquid-cooled cables: 500–700 A through a hand-held cable would need absurdly thick copper — unless coolant carries the I²R heat away. Megawatt-class stacks (960–1,280 kW, up to 16 connectors) target trucks and fleet depots, where EU rules mandating 45-minute driver rest breaks define the charging window.

V2G (vehicle-to-grid) just means the charger's rectifier becomes bidirectional — a parked EV becomes a small storage plant. Same electronics as a PCS; the barriers are standards and billing, not physics.

MICROGRIDS are small grids that can island: when the main grid dies, a grid-forming converter (VSG) becomes the local metronome, holding voltage and frequency for a factory, campus, or island — handling unbalanced loads (heavy on one phase) and coordinating 100+ paralleled units. Battery-agnostic DC inputs (lithium, sodium-ion, even flywheels) hedge whatever chemistry wins.

Data centers are converging on the same ideas: AI halls are moving toward high-voltage DC distribution (HVDC) and solid-state transformers (SST) — power electronics replacing iron transformers — and meanwhile buy harmonic filters, SVGs, and sag protection for their existing AC halls. One more industry adopting the same building block.

sections.heading: 5 · Industry Map — Who Buys, Who Competes, Why Modular Wins
bullets: Different buyers per product line, one platform underneath: storage PCS sells to battery-system integrators and project developers (who buy conversion rather than build it); power quality sells to factories, semiconductor fabs, data centers, and ships; chargers sell to charge-point operators, fleets, and automakers' station programs; charging modules sell merchant to other charger builders; battery test systems sell to cell factories.

The third-party PCS position: giant vertically-integrated inverter makers (Sungrow-class) sell whole storage systems — competing with the very integrators who need PCS. A PCS specialist that does NOT sell complete systems is a safe supplier for integrators, competing on module architecture, overload headroom, reliability, and certification breadth rather than on owning the whole project.

Certification IS the product at utility scale: every country's grid code (EN 50549, UL 1741/IEEE 1547, national variants) must be individually certified, and bankability lists (BloombergNEF Tier 1) decide whose hardware project financiers will accept. A big certification portfolio is a moat measured in years of lab queues.

Why modular architecture matters strategically: one power-electronics building block — a SiC converter module — amortizes R&D across storage, power quality, EV charging, battery test, and now data-center power. Field economics follow: swap a module in minutes instead of craning out a monolithic inverter, add capacity in 62.5–215 kVA steps, and keep the plant running on N-1 modules.

Watch the concept, not the noise: as renewables displace spinning generators, grid-forming capability moves from premium feature to tender requirement — the companies that industrialized VSG early ride that regulatory wave. The same power-electronics competence is simultaneously being pulled into AI data centers (HVDC/SST), making 'who else needs a fast, efficient AC↔DC box' the recurring strategic question.

flashcards.q: What does a PCS (power conversion system) do in a battery storage plant?
flashcards.a: It is the bidirectional AC↔DC gateway between the DC battery and the AC grid: an inverter when discharging, a rectifier when charging. It also executes grid commands (frequency regulation, ramping) in milliseconds and rides through grid faults — the batteries just store energy; the PCS does everything else.

flashcards.q: Why do storage systems keep pushing DC voltage up (e.g. 1,040–1,500 V battery windows)?
flashcards.a: P = V·I and wire losses scale with I²R. Higher voltage moves the same power with less current — less copper, less heat, higher efficiency. The same logic drives 800 V EV packs and high-voltage DC distribution in data centers.

flashcards.q: Grid-following vs grid-forming inverter — what's the difference?
flashcards.a: Grid-following is a surfer: it locks onto the grid's existing voltage wave and injects current — useless if the grid is dead. Grid-forming is a metronome: it creates the voltage and frequency itself, others sync to it. Forming enables off-grid operation, black start, and grid stability as spinning generators retire.

flashcards.q: What is VSG (virtual synchronous generator) mode?
flashcards.a: A control mode where a grid-forming converter imitates a heavy spinning generator — providing synthetic inertia that resists frequency changes. It replaces the stabilizing mass the grid loses when coal/gas plants close, and lets 100+ converters share an islanded grid in parallel.

flashcards.q: What are harmonics and why are they harmful?
flashcards.a: Current distortion at multiples of the grid frequency, created by loads that draw current in gulps (rectifiers, drives, server PSUs). Harmonics overheat transformers and neutral conductors, trip breakers, and distort the voltage other equipment sees. THD is the score; <5% is the common target.

flashcards.q: How does an active harmonic filter (APF/AHF) clean up a factory's power?
flashcards.a: Like noise-cancelling headphones: it measures the distorted current in real time and injects the exact mirror-image waveform, so distortion cancels and the grid sees a clean sine wave. It's a fast inverter running a cancellation algorithm.

flashcards.q: What is reactive power, and what does power factor measure?
flashcards.a: Reactive power is magnetizing current that sloshes between source and load doing no net work — but still occupying wires and transformers. Power factor = useful power ÷ apparent power; utilities penalize low PF because it wastes their infrastructure capacity.

flashcards.q: Why did inverter-based SVGs replace capacitor banks for power-factor correction?
flashcards.a: Capacitor banks switch in coarse, slow steps and can resonate with harmonics. An SVG is an inverter that generates exactly the reactive current needed, steplessly, in ~15 ms, reaching PF 0.99 — and the same hardware platform can also balance phases and regulate voltage.

flashcards.q: What is a voltage sag, and how does an active voltage conditioner protect against it?
flashcards.a: A dip in grid voltage lasting a few cycles (lightning, faults, big motor starts). Precision loads like semiconductor tools can scrap product from a 100 ms sag. The conditioner keeps a charged supercapacitor bank and a standby inverter that injects the missing voltage within ~2 ms — even a dip to zero volts is bridged for a few seconds.

flashcards.q: Why do supercapacitors, not batteries, back a voltage-sag protector?
flashcards.a: Sags last milliseconds to seconds and need huge power instantly, not much energy. Supercapacitors deliver extreme power density and millions of cycles without wearing out; batteries store more energy but respond and age worse for this duty. Match the storage physics to the event timescale.

flashcards.q: Why does overload capability (e.g. 1.5×) matter in a PCS datasheet?
flashcards.a: During faults, breakers need a surge of current to trip cleanly; off-grid, motors draw several times rated current at start. A PCS with headroom can deliver that surge briefly; one without it stalls or trips exactly when the system needs it most.

flashcards.q: What is a DC fast-charging module, and why are chargers built from stacks of them?
flashcards.a: A 20–40 kW AC→DC rectifier brick with a wide output window (≈50–1,000 V to cover 400 V and 800 V packs). Paralleling modules scales power (24 × 20 kW ≈ 480 kW), gives redundancy (one fails, the rest carry on), and lets software allocate modules dynamically to whichever car can absorb power.

flashcards.q: Why do megawatt-class charging cables need liquid cooling?
flashcards.a: I²R: at 500–700 A, a hand-holdable cable would overheat unless coolant carries the heat away — thicker copper alone would make the cable unusable. Liquid cooling lets high current flow through a manageable cable, enabling 10-minute truck and car charging.

flashcards.q: What is V2G, in power-electronics terms?
flashcards.a: Making the charger's AC→DC conversion bidirectional so a parked EV can discharge to the grid — functionally turning car + charger into a small storage plant with a PCS. The physics is identical to stationary storage; the hard parts are standards, billing, and battery-warranty rules.

flashcards.q: Why does modular converter architecture matter beyond marketing?
flashcards.a: One building-block module amortizes R&D across storage PCS, harmonic filters, SVGs, EV charging, and data-center power; in the field it means capacity added in small steps, failed modules swapped in minutes instead of craning out a monolith, and N+1-style availability. Architecture, not any single spec, is the durable advantage.
